label: Bank statements to journal entries
description: Read a bank statement PDF, work out who each payment was to or from, classify it, and produce journal entries that provably foot. Specified by docs/backend-model-evaluation.md.

documents.describe: Seven bank statements, one per account, four currencies, six business days

passes.name: extract
prompt: You are parsing a bank statement PDF into transaction rows for a fund administrator.
Write a Python file, `parse.py`. The `kit` module gives you:
kit.page_count() -> int
kit.lines(page)  -> visual lines on that page, top to bottom.
PAGES ARE 1-BASED: iterate range(1, kit.page_count()+1).
Each line has:
line.text                  str  — the whole line
line.words                 list[dict] — each with "text" and "x0"
line.between(a, b)         str  — the text of that column,
ALREADY JOINED. Not a list.
line.words_between(a, b)   list[dict] — the words themselves
kit.column_positions() -> dict of the left edge of every column, read from
the statement's own header row:
bank_reference, customer_reference, trn_type,
value_date, credit, debit, balance, time, post_date
kit.write_result(rows) -> writes /work/result.json
Each row is a dict with these keys:
bank_reference, trn_type, value_date, post_date, time, narrative,
credit, debit, balance, account_number, currency, page
Amounts are strings, no thousands separators, sign exactly as printed. Exactly
one of credit/debit is set; the other is None. Rows in statement order, newest
first.
## What statements actually look like
- **They span several pages, and the transactions continue across them.** The
column header row repeats at the top of every page; so does the "Statement
details" block. Skip the furniture, keep the transactions, and keep them in
page order — a row dropped at a page boundary breaks the chain by exactly
the amount of that row.
- Day boundaries appear *between* transactions as "Balance as at close <date>"
and "Balance brought forward <date>". They are markers, not transactions,
and their amount sits in a different column from the transaction balances.
- The narrative is a continuation line under its transaction, labelled
`Narrative`. The bank wraps long names mid-word by inserting a comma, so
"NORDVIK INFRASTR, UCTURE V SCSP" is one name, not two.

checks.name: balance_chain
checks.describe: a row's balance minus its amount must equal the NEXT row's balance

checks.name: closing_balance
checks.describe: the first row's balance equals the closing balance printed on page 1

checks.name: printed_openings
checks.describe: every "Balance brought forward" marker must reproduce from the movements

checks.name: row_count
checks.describe: one row per transaction. "Balance as at close" and "Balance brought forward" are day markers, NOT transactions

checks.name: reference_provenance
checks.describe: every bank_reference appears literally in the PDF text

text: `line.between(a, b)` returns a **string**; `line.words_between(a, b)` returns
the word dicts. Writing `" ".join(w["text"] for w in line.between(a, b))`
iterates the characters of a string and raises TypeError — that mistake cost
two earlier runs every attempt they had.
This statement prints no "Balance brought forward" marker at all, so
`printed_openings` will come back UNRESOLVED. That is expected and does not
block acceptance — do not invent a marker to satisfy it.
`bank_reference` must appear **literally** in the PDF. Join words with a single
space where the document has one and with nothing where it does not. Two
failure shapes to avoid: a space between every character, and stripping all
spaces so the next column's text runs into the reference.

passes.name: resolve
prompt: The transaction rows have already been extracted and their arithmetic verified.
Your job is to resolve each row against the reference lists and classify it.
Write a Python file, `resolve.py`. The `kit` module gives you:
kit.rows()                    -> the extracted rows, as dicts
kit.tables()                  -> the names of the reference lists
kit.lookup(value, pools, markers) -> USE THIS. Finds `value` in the first
pool that holds it, applying every repair
below for you. Returns
{matched_name, table, column, tried} or None.
`pools` is [(table, column), ...] in the order
you want tried; `markers` is the suffix list.
kit.trim_to(text, markers)    -> cut a string at the first marker, keeping it
kit.variants(text)            -> the readings of a line-wrapped value
kit.narrative_span(narrative, name) -> the slice of the narrative that name
corresponds to, EXACTLY as the document wrote
it. Use it for every `_raw` field you emit.
kit.fold(text) / kit.compact(text)  -> comparison keys, accent- and
case-insensitive
t = kit.table(name)
t.columns / t.contains(col, v) / t.find(col, v) / t.values(col)
t.candidates(col, v, n)     -> near matches, ranked, for PROPOSING only
kit.write_result(rows)        -> writes /work/result.json
**Do not hand-roll normalisation, comma-unwrapping or a variant ladder.**
`kit.lookup` already does all of it — accents, case, the bank's wrap comma in
either position, and a qualifier the list adds that the document omits
(`NISC ApS - Non-LU` where the narrative says `NISC APS`). Every previous run
rewrote these by hand and roughly half got them subtly wrong.
The lists available, and a sensible order to try them:
related_parties  Related Party
vendors          Vendor
investors        Investor
legal_entities   Legal Entity
deals_positions  Deal Name, Position
Emit every input row, in the same order, with these keys added and every
original key kept unchanged:
counterparty_raw     the party's name exactly as the narrative writes it,
or null if the narrative names none
counterparty_match   {status, matched_name, table, confidence, why}
project_code_raw     the project word exactly as written, or null
project_code_match   {status, matched_name, table, confidence, why}
classification       one of the labels listed below
`status` is one of:
MATCH          `kit.lookup` found it. Copy `matched_name` and `table` from
what it returned — the list's spelling, not the document's.
PROBABLE       lookup failed, but a candidate is obviously the same thing.
Give `matched_name` (from `t.candidates`, so it is a real
list entry), `table`, a `confidence` strictly between 0 and 1,
and a `why` saying what differed. See below.
UNRESOLVED     a name was read out of the narrative and nothing plausible
was found. Keep `counterparty_raw`; `matched_name` is null.
CANNOT_VERIFY  the narrative names nobody, so there was nothing to look up.
FAIL           the row is malformed and you cannot proceed.
## Where a name ends — read this twice
This is the one thing previous runs got wrong, every time, and it cost a
quarter of the rows.
**A party name ends at its legal-form token.** `SCSP`, `S.C.Sp`, `Ltd`,
`Limited`, `ApS`, `A/S`, `K/S`, `P/S`, `GmbH`, `U.A.`, `S.à r.l.`, `Pte Ltd`,
`Inc`, `BV`, `NV`. Everything after it is why the money moved, not who was paid.
... PMT FRM NI ABF II SCSP TO NI ABF I, SCSP FOR PURCHASE 100PER OF ACC INT ...
counterparty_raw   everything after `SCSP`
is purpose text
Do not bound the span by looking for words like PROJECT or REF and cutting
there — those appear at the very end of the narrative, so the span swallows the
whole clause. Bound it POSITIVELY at the legal-form token. `kit.trim_to` does
exactly this, and `kit.lookup` calls it for you.
Four more things the bank does, each of which broke a previous run:
- **It writes `PMT FRM`, not `FROM`.** A `\bFROM\b` regex silently never fires
and you fall through to a weaker path. Match `FRM` too.
- **The wrap comma can land on the delimiter**: `... SCSP TO, NI GMF II ...`.
A pattern needing whitespace after `TO` misses it and captures both parties
as one string.
- **`\bTO\b` case-insensitively also matches the English preposition** in
`related to contri. 5`. One run captured twenty-one words that way.
- **Strip a leading `TO`, `FROM`, `FRM`, `PMT`, `OBO`, `1/` or `BENEFICIARY:`**
before looking a name up.
Emit `counterparty_raw` using `kit.narrative_span(narrative, matched_name)` so
it is the document's own characters. That is what the provenance check reads.
## Proposing, when it is obviously the same company
A narrative saying `NI V KALVIK TOPCO LTD.` against a list holding
`NI V Kalvik Topco Limited` is the same company, and throwing it away as
UNRESOLVED leaves a person to work it out from nothing. Offer it:
{"status": "PROBABLE", "matched_name": "NI V Kalvik Topco Limited",
"table": "legal_entities", "confidence": 0.8,
"why": "the narrative abbreviates the legal form; Ltd. and Limited"}
Differences small enough to propose: trailing punctuation, an abbreviated or
spelled-out legal form, the bank's wrap comma, case or accents, a qualifier the
list adds. A proposal is never applied — it routes to a person with the answer
already filled in.
**Differences that are NOT small, and must stay UNRESOLVED:**
- a different entity number or numeral — `NI V` and `NI IV` are different
companies, and so are `NI ABF I` and `NI ABF II`
- a different currency or jurisdiction where the rest also differs
- anything you cannot state a one-line reason for
Never propose from `t.candidates` without reading the candidate and satisfying
yourself. A wrong proposal costs a reviewer a click; a wrong MATCH goes into
the accounts.
## The counterparty is the other party
A narrative often names both sides: `LOAN: FROM NI V SCSP TO NI V AZURITE
HOLDCO LIMITED`. The account these rows came from belongs to one of them, and
**that one is not the counterparty**. Take the other. Each row carries its own
`account_number`, and the statement's own entity is the name that recurs on
nearly every row of the account — if a candidate is that entity, you have
picked the wrong side of the sentence.
## Which list to prefer
The same entity can appear on more than one list under different forms —
`NI V CN SCSp` on the related party master and `Nordvik Infrastructure V CN
SCSp` on the legal entity master are the same company. Try the lists in this
order and stop at the first hit, because the later stages want the related
party form where one exists:
related_parties -> vendors -> investors -> legal_entities -> deals_positions
A list entry may carry a qualifier the narrative never writes — a currency or
a jurisdiction, as in `NI GMF II Coöperatief U.A. - USD` or `NISC ApS - Non-LU`.
`kit.lookup` recognises the name without it and returns the entry **as the list
holds it**, qualifier included. Keep what it returns; do not trim it back to
what the narrative said, because the qualifier is how later stages tell two
currency sleeves of the same company apart.
## The project code
The project word is in the narrative, usually straight after the word
`PROJECT` — `... PROJECT CEPHALUS`, `... PROJECT WILLOWBANK`. Take the single
token after it. Unlike a party name, a project code has no spaces, so bound it
at the first whitespace; that is why this step has always resolved far better
than the counterparty one, and it is worth not breaking.
If the narrative names no project, that is CANNOT_VERIFY — many rows have none.
Resolve the word with `kit.lookup(word, [('project_codes', 'Project Code'),
('project_codes', 'New Project Code')])`, and pass no suffix markers: legal-form
tokens are for party names and would cut a project code in half.
Do not let a party name leak into the project lookup, or a project code into
the counterparty lookup. Blank out the counterparty span before searching for
the project word if that is easier.
## Build the journal lines, and check them yourself
Add `journal_lines` to every row: two lines sharing a `batch`, the cash side
and the counterparty side, equal and opposite.
{"batch": "<row id>", "amount": "301908.70", "is_debit": true,
"transaction_type": "Payable - Third Party"}
`amount` is always positive; direction is carried by `is_debit` and never by
the transaction type. In this data every cash leg reads `Cash - Disbursed`
including the credits, so a sign taken from the type name is wrong on a
quarter of the rows.
**This gives you something to check yourself.** Call
`kit.batches_balance(rows)` before you write the result. It returns
`{ok, batches, balanced, problems}`. If `ok` is false, fix the rows — a
rejected attempt costs a whole generation and this costs nothing.
Then record what you checked with `kit.write_assertions([...])`:
kit.write_assertions([
{"name": "batches_balance", "holds": r["ok"], "detail": f"{r['balanced']}/{r['batches']}"},
{"name": "spans_are_short", "holds": longest <= 8, "detail": f"longest {longest} words"},
Be honest in these. A claim that does not hold fails the attempt and its
detail reaches your next prompt, which is the fastest way to fix something.
A claim that does hold changes nothing on its own — it cannot make an attempt
pass that the real checks rejected — so there is nothing to gain by claiming
something you have not checked, and real value in saying plainly what is off.
## Classification
`classification` must be exactly one of these eight strings, copied verbatim.
Nothing else is accepted, and a label of your own invention fails the run:
Investment            buying or selling a position, or funding one directly
Investment Transfer   money moved between two of the platform's own entities
in order to fund or settle an investment. Most rows
whose narrative says FROM one entity TO another and
then names a project are this, even though the
counterparty is also on the related party list
Vendor                paying a supplier
Related Party         a movement with a related party that is not funding
an investment — a fee, a rebate, a settling of
balances. Being on the related party list does not by
itself make a row this
Investor              a capital call or distribution
Internal              a transfer between the platform's own accounts
Other                 bank charges, interest, and anything routine
Review                none of the above
Whether an investment row is equity or a loan is carried by the narrative —
shares and equity on one side, loan principal and accrued interest on the
other — but that distinction belongs in the position, not in this label.
**Classification comes from the narrative, not from whether a lookup
succeeded.** A row whose counterparty is UNRESOLVED is still classifiable: the
narrative says what kind of movement it is regardless of whether the name is on
a list. `Review` is for a row you genuinely cannot place — in this week's data
that is about three rows in a hundred, not most of them. A commission or a bank
charge is `Other`; a transfer between the platform's own accounts is `Internal`;
a loan or purchase to a named entity is `Investment` or `Investment Transfer`.
Reaching for `Review` because the counterparty did not resolve is the mistake to
avoid; a made-up label is the other one.

checks.name: provenance
checks.describe: a counterparty you claim to have pulled out must appear in that row's narrative

checks.name: membership
checks.describe: a MATCH must name a list and a value that is really in it

checks.name: completeness
checks.describe: every row carries a status for both — an omitted resolution is unexamined, not unresolved

checks.name: vocabulary
checks.describe: the classification must be one of the declared labels

checks.name: span
checks.describe: an extracted name must look like a name, not like a sentence

checks.name: proposals
checks.describe: a PROBABLE must carry a reason and a confidence between 0 and 1

checks.name: label_rate
checks.describe: Review is the label of last resort; it should be rare

checks.name: double_entry
checks.describe: two lines per batch, equal and opposite — the arithmetic you can check yourself

text: Caution belongs in the **matching**, not in the reading. Two different jobs:
- `counterparty_raw` and `project_code_raw` are *transcription*. If the
narrative names a party or a project, copy it out — always, whether or not
any list contains it. Leaving it null claims the narrative named nobody,
which is a different and usually wrong statement, and it robs the reviewer
of the one thing they need to decide the row.
- The `_match` status is *judgement*, and there you are strict. Forcing an
unmatched name to the nearest list entry is the single worst thing you can
do here: an UNRESOLVED row goes to a person, a wrong match goes into the
accounts. Never use `candidates` to pick a match.
So a narrative naming `NI V KALVIK TOPCO LTD.` that is in no list gives
`counterparty_raw` set and status UNRESOLVED. Only a narrative that names no
party at all — a bank charge, an interest posting — gives null and
CANNOT_VERIFY. In this week's data roughly half the rows name somebody, and
about half of those resolve.
A `counterparty_raw` must be a literal substring of that row's own narrative.
Copy it out rather than reconstructing it, and if the narrative names nobody,
set it to null with status CANNOT_VERIFY.
The classification must be one of the eight strings listed above, copied
exactly. Not a variation, not a refinement, not a hyphenated pair — if the
row is an equity purchase the label is still `Investment`, and if none of
the eight fits, it is `Review`.
A MATCH has to name the list it came from and the value as that list holds
it. Use `t.find(col, v)` and read the value back out of the row it returns,
rather than echoing what the narrative said. If `find` returns None, the
status is UNRESOLVED.
The span ran past the end of the name. A party name ends at its legal-form
token — SCSP, Ltd, Limited, ApS, A/S, K/S, U.A., S.à r.l. — and everything
after it is why the money moved. Use `kit.trim_to(text, markers)`, or just
call `kit.lookup(value, pools, markers)`, which trims before it searches.
Too many rows fell through to `Review`. It is the label of last resort, not
the answer when a lookup failed — a bank charge is `Other` and a transfer
between the platform's own accounts is `Internal` whether or not the
counterparty resolved. Decide from the narrative's verbs.
A batch did not net to zero. Call `kit.batches_balance(rows)` before writing
the result and fix what it reports — it is the same arithmetic the verifier
runs, so there is no reason to find out afterwards.
